new_statements.quote: /i/ is realised as in English 'me', 'see', 'machine' (a high close front vowel) in open syllables; in closed syllables it is realised as in English 'bit', 'fit' (a high open front vowel). This is roughly the same distribution as for English. Note that stress normally falls on the penultimate syllable in Bislama. Examples: mi, 'me'; bitim, 'to beat'; kilim, 'to hit'; pinklos, 'clothes peg'; singaot, 'to call out'.
new_statements.citation: Tryon, Darrell T. 1987. Bislama: An Introduction to the National Language of Vanuatu. Pacific Linguistics D-72. Canberra: Research School of Pacific Studies, Australian National University. DOI 10.15144/PL-D72.

Guy 1974 PL C-34 p. 6 (PDF p.…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress normally falls on the second-to-last syllable (Tryon gives this as a one-sentence norm, with 'normally' hedging; no further rules or exceptions are given anywhere in the book).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing said by Tryon. Guy 1974 (p. 6) describes words of three or more syllables as having 'only their first and last syllables stressed' and otherwise even stress on every syllable, i.e. no primary/secondary hierarchy.
new_statements.exceptions: Tryon: none beyond 'normally'. The older Guy 1974 Handbook of Bichelamar (PL C-34, p. 6, also saved) gives a conflicting, diffuse account: 'Correctly placing the stress in Bichelamar has not the same importance as it has in English, as misplacing it will never lead to confusions between words, and as stress is very often evenly distributed over the syllables of the words'; monosyllabic tool-words (mi, long, we) unstressed; 'Two-syllable verbs ending in em, im or um have usually only their first syllable stressed' (tékem, kílim, púsum -- which coincides with penult); 'Words of more than two syllables have most often only their first and last syllables stressed' (ólketá, túvalá, námaláo); 'Otherwise, the stress falls evenly on every syllable of the word'.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level, citation forms; Tryon's remark is embedded in the segmental description of a second-language pidgin/creole whose pronunciation he says varies with the speaker's vernacular (p. 12). Stress is non-contrastive per Guy 1974.
new_statements.identity_note: Both saved sources describe general Vanuatu Bislama (bisl1239; Guy 1974 under the older name 'Bichelamar'). Tryon notes pronunciation varies by speakers' vernacular (L2 variety for most speakers in 1987); no particular dialect singled out.

new_statements.quote: Almost all disyllables and words of four or more syllables take stress on the penultimate syllable and on each alternate syllable to the left of the penult. Exceptions will be discussed below; the following, however, give evidence of the fairly general application of this rule: (6) [kála] 'colour' [lóto] 'motor vehicle' [máket] 'market' [nákatámbol] 'kind of tree' [nátakúra] 'sago' [nákavíka] 'Malay-apple' (p. 193) ... Stress in Bislama is thus basically of an alternating pattern, with stress falling on the penultimate syllable and each alternate syllable to the left of it. Exceptional words, like those in (7) and (9) through (11) should be so marked in the dictionary. (p. 195)

new_statements.relation_note: Agrees with the catalog rule (penultimate: penultimate stress) and with Tryon 1987's 'stress normally falls on the penultimate syllable'. Refines it by (a) stating an alternating leftward secondary-stress pattern from the penult, (b) listing lexical exception classes (-ap final stress; -fala/-vala initial; English-retained and local-origin initial trisyllables; initial+final in some complex words), and (c) noting idiolectal variation from substrate and superstrate languages. It explicitly refutes Guy 1974's 'first and last syllables' / 'evenly on every syllable' description (Guy already held by the project in this folder), which the catalog does not follow anyway.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress on the penultimate syllable, with further stresses on every alternate syllable leftward from the penult (a right-to-left trochaic alternating pattern). Monosyllables are stressed except grammatical morphemes (p. 193). Lynch rejects Guy 1974's rules [C] (first and last syllables in 3+ syllable words) and [D] (even stress on every syllable) as contradictory and phonologically inaccurate, while accepting Guy's rules [A] (unstressed monosyllabic function words) and [B] (-em/-im/-um disyllabic verbs stressed initially, which is penultimate anyway). Diphthong-final words stress the first vowel of the diphthong ([kakái], [námarái], [kátemdáun]), consistent with penultimate placement if diphthongs are vowel clusters; words with non-final diphthongs ([kapsáitem], not *[kápsaítem]) need a stress-shift rule (p. 195).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Yes, explicit: 'on each alternate syllable to the left of the penult' (p. 193, p. 195), e.g. [nákatámbol] 'kind of tree', [nátakúra] 'sago', [nákavíka] 'Malay-apple'. Lynch does not distinguish primary from secondary stress notationally; all are marked with the acute.
new_statements.exceptions: (7) Words ending in -ap (from English 'up') always take final stress: [antáp] 'up, above', [bágaráp] 'broken', [klosáp] 'close, near' (p. 194). (9) Trisyllables in the suffix -fala ~ -vala show initial stress: [mífala] 'we (excl.)', [túfala] 'the two of them', [bíkfala] 'big (emphatic)' (p. 194). (10) Some initially-stressed trisyllables retained the English stress pattern ([kámbani] 'group', [péntekos] 'Pentecost Island', [kálabus] 'jail') and some words of local origin have initial stress ([nákamal] 'men's house', [nángalat] 'stinging tree') (p. 194). (11) Some trisyllables that are complex in the source language stress initial and final syllables: [évriwán] 'everyone', [stórián] 'talk, chat', [bákegén] 'again' (p. 194). Fn. 12 (p. 203): 'there is a certain amount of idiolectal variation in stress patterns, due largely to (a) the stress patterns of the individual's native language, and (b) the stress patterns of English or French, in idiolects of speakers with a certain degree of fluency in one of these languages.' Fn. 2 (p. 201): the name Bislama itself is 'stress sometimes penultimate, sometimes final'.
new_statements.identity_note: Lynch describes Bislama of the New Hebrides (Vanuatu) generally, drawing on Tanna (Southern District) data for the obstruent discussion; he treats Bislama, Solomon Islands Pidgin and Tok Pisin as dialects of one language (p. 189) but the stress data are Bislama. Fn. 12 flags idiolectal (substrate/superstrate-driven) variation in stress rather than a named dialect.

readall_conflicts: Lynch 1975 (penultimate with leftward alternation, plus lexical exceptions) agrees with Tryon 1987 (penultimate) and with the catalog. The only disagreement in the folder is with Guy 1974 (Handbook of Bichelamar, sec. 6 'Stress', p. 6), which claims stress is of minor importance, that words of more than two syllables 'have most often only their first and last syllables stressed' and that otherwise 'stress falls evenly on every syllable'; Lynch quotes these rules and rejects them as internally contradictory and phonologically inaccurate (pp. 192-193). Lynch also notes real idiolectal variation (fn. 12, p. 203) and that even the language name is 'stress sometimes penultimate, sometimes final' (fn. 2, p. 201), so the penultimate rule is a strong default with marked exceptions rather than exceptionless.

sources.note: Fullest open first-hand account of Bislama word stress (sec. 1.2, pp. 192-195): penultimate primary stress with alternating secondary stress leftward, plus enumerated lexical exception classes (-ap final, -fala initial, English-retained initial). Explicitly refutes Guy 1974's 'even stress' rules and corroborates Tryon 1987's penult norm; should be cited alongside Tryon in the catalog entry.

sources.note: Section #6 'Stress', p. 6 (French '#6 L'accent tonique', pp. 60-61): stress placement 'has not the same importance as it has in English.. stress is very often evenly distributed over the syllables'; monosyllabic tool-words unstressed; disyllabic verbs in -em/-im/-um stress the first syllable (tekem, kilim, pusum); words of 3+ syllables 'most often only their first and last syllables stressed' (olketa, tuvala, namalao); otherwise 'stress falls evenly on every syllable' (kala, nakatambol).
